# Revenue Architecture — Full Section 6 Walkthrough

Most brands describe what they sell. Few brands describe how their revenue actually compounds. The difference is whether the brand survives the founder taking a month off.

This walkthrough produces 6 outputs. The model works for personal brands, agencies, and product companies — the layers stay the same, only the offer types change.

---

## 6.1 Service / offer pillars

**Pillars are problem-shapes, not services.**

Wrong:
- Logo design
- Website design
- Brand audit

Right:
- Foundation work — for businesses with no brand, lock the brand foundation in 4-6 weeks.
- Refresh work — for businesses with a stale brand, modernize the system without losing equity.
- Activation work — for businesses with a locked brand, help them ship campaigns / content / launches that use it.

The wrong list describes deliverables. The right list describes problems the brand solves. Pillars are problems; offers are solutions inside pillars.

**Format per pillar:**

```markdown
### {Pillar name}

**The problem:**
What's broken in the customer's world that this pillar solves.

**Who needs it:**
The specific stage / situation that triggers this need.

**What we deliver:**
The high-level deliverable shape (not the line items).

**The signal that the engagement worked:**
The outcome the customer can name 90 days later.
```

Typically 3–5 pillars. Fewer than 3 = brand is too narrow to compound. More than 5 = brand is unfocused, drifts.

---

## 6.2 Signature offers — the ladder

A ladder of 3–7 offers from low-commitment to high-commitment. Each rung serves a different stage of customer relationship.

**Ladder shape (typical for service brands):**

| Rung | Commitment | Price band | Format | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Free | $0 | Lead magnet, newsletter, free template | Establish credibility, capture audience |
| 2 | Low | $50-$500 | Workshop, mini-course, paid consult | Convert audience to buyer |
| 3 | Medium | $1K-$10K | Productized service, intensive engagement | Deliver real outcome at fixed scope |
| 4 | High | $10K-$100K | Custom engagement, retainer | Long-term partnership |
| 5 | Premium | $100K+ | Equity, partnership, exclusive engagement | High-leverage, high-trust work |

**Per-offer documentation:**

```markdown
### {Offer name}

- **Format:** {workshop / coaching / done-for-you / done-with-you / product / etc.}
- **Length:** {hours / weeks / open-ended}
- **Price:** ${amount} or "Request quote" + the signal that triggers a quote
- **Who it's for:** the persona + stage
- **What it produces:** the deliverable the customer can name
- **What it does NOT include:** scope guards (so scope creep is named)
- **The lead-in:** which lower rung typically precedes this offer
- **The lead-out:** which higher rung this offer typically leads to
```

**Anti-pattern:** brands with 12 offers, none of which compound. The ladder discipline forces consolidation: every offer must make a different ladder rung make sense.

---

## 6.3 The full revenue model — three layers

Real revenue compounding has three layers stacked. A brand with only one layer caps out at the founder's hours.

### Layer 1 — Active revenue (trade time at high rates)

Hours billed for work done. Consulting, custom projects, retainers.

**Constraints:**
- Maximum: founder hours/week × billable rate
- Margin: typically 70–90% (low overhead, no inventory)
- Risk: ceiling-bound, churn-vulnerable, founder-dependent

**Document:**
- Specific offers in this layer
- Hourly / daily / project rates
- Maximum billable hours target per week
- Utilization target (typically 60-70% — never 100%)

### Layer 2 — Leveraged revenue (your time reaches more people)

Time still spent, but reaches more people per hour. Cohorts, group coaching, paid speaking, courses delivered live, workshops.

**Constraints:**
- Maximum: cohort size × seats × cadence
- Margin: typically 50–80%
- Risk: requires audience at top of funnel, requires repeatable curriculum

**Document:**
- Specific offers in this layer
- Cohort size + cadence
- Required pre-work / qualification
- The funnel that fills cohorts (where do leads come from?)

### Layer 3 — Passive / automated revenue (builds once, runs without the founder)

Self-paced courses, books, products, license-able templates, software, paid memberships.

**Constraints:**
- Maximum: market size × conversion rate (no founder bottleneck)
- Margin: typically 80–95% after build cost amortizes
- Risk: high upfront investment, may not earn out, requires marketing engine

**Document:**
- Specific offers in this layer
- Build cost (time + money)
- Expected break-even point
- The marketing engine that drives volume

### The cardinal rule

A brand with ONLY Layer 1 has a job, not a business. A brand with ONLY Layer 3 (no proof from active work) sounds like a guru. The compounding brand operates ALL THREE layers, with Layer 1 producing proof, Layer 2 producing repeatability, and Layer 3 producing scale.

---

## 6.4 The automation architecture

The "money machine" layer connects offers to systems. Without this, every revenue layer needs the founder to manually fulfill it.

**Components to document:**

### CRM
- Tool used (HubSpot, GoHighLevel, Pipedrive, etc.)
- Pipeline stages
- Required fields per opportunity
- Automated follow-up sequences (cadence, content)

### Scheduling
- Tool (Calendly, Cal.com, Google Calendar native)
- Available windows per offer
- Buffer rules (no back-to-back calls, no meetings before X time)
- Booking links per offer (different intake forms per offer)

### Payments
- Tool (Stripe, Paypal, GHL Payments, etc.)
- Payment terms per offer (net-30, deposit-then-balance, monthly)
- Refund policy (and the mechanism)
- Invoicing automation

### Fulfillment
- Per offer: who does the work, what tools, what deliverable templates
- Status updates to the customer (cadence, format)
- Final hand-off ritual (call, doc, recording)

### Follow-up
- Post-engagement: testimonial request, case-study build, referral request
- Re-engagement sequences (at 90 days, 6 months, 1 year)

**The automation goal:** anything that's done identically across every customer should be automated. The founder's time is reserved for the work that only the founder can do.

---

## 6.5 Revenue timeline (phased)

A quarter-by-quarter roadmap of which revenue layers come online and when.

**Format:**

```markdown
### Q1 {YEAR}
- **Active layer:** {specific offers, target revenue}
- **Leveraged layer:** {what's being built — workshops, cohorts}
- **Passive layer:** {what's being researched / drafted}
- **Milestone:** {the gate that unlocks Q2}

### Q2 {YEAR}
- **Active layer:** {now stable, focus on retention}
- **Leveraged layer:** {first cohort / first paid speaking gig}
- **Passive layer:** {first product in beta}
- **Milestone:** {the gate that unlocks Q3}
```

The phased timeline keeps the brand from over-extending. A brand that tries to launch all three layers at once usually launches none of them well.

---

## 6.6 Lead → client journey

The exact path from "first awareness" to "signed contract." Every touchpoint named, every CTA mapped to a stage.

**Format:**

```markdown
### Stage 1 — First touch
- **Where they encounter us:** {specific surfaces — search, social, podcast, referral, speaking}
- **What they see:** {the lead-in content — blog post, social post, podcast episode}
- **The CTA:** {specific action — subscribe, download, follow, listen}

### Stage 2 — Audience member
- **Where they live:** {newsletter list, follower list}
- **What we send them:** {regular cadence content}
- **The CTA:** {specific action — RSVP to workshop, book a consult, reply to a question}

### Stage 3 — Qualified lead
- **The trigger:** {signal that they're ready to buy}
- **What we send:** {qualification call, proposal, scoping doc}
- **The CTA:** {specific action — book the call, sign the proposal}

### Stage 4 — Active client
- **What we do:** {fulfillment workflow}
- **The CTA at end:** {referral, testimonial, repeat engagement}

### Stage 5 — Past client
- **The cadence:** {re-engagement schedule}
- **The CTA:** {specific action — refer a peer, re-engage at higher tier}
```

Every CTA in this journey appears in the messaging framework's CTA inventory (Section 5). If a CTA is in the journey but not the inventory, that's a gap to fix.

---

## What this walkthrough does NOT do

- Does not pick prices for the user. It documents how the brand thinks about prices and asks the user to set them.
- Does not invent customers. The lead-to-client journey only documents real / actively-pursued segments.
- Does not promise multi-layer revenue is achievable in any specific timeline. The phased timeline is the user's plan, not a guarantee.
- Does not exclude founder-led service businesses from the model. Even a single-founder consultancy benefits from naming the three layers, even if Layer 3 is "deferred to year 3."
